props.title: Sorority Row
props.initialSlug: A deadly secret, a deadly price.

sections.content: Sorority Row (2009) fits squarely into the late 2000s slasher revival trend, following films like Prom Night (2008) and My Bloody Valentine 3D (2009). This remake-adjacent film (loosely based on 1983's The House on Sorority Row) updates the formula with digital age touches - viral videos, text message threats, and cyberbullying become central plot devices. The film follows a familiar slasher template: a prank gone wrong leads to death, followed by a cover-up that comes back to haunt the perpetrators. What sets it apart is its self-aware approach to Greek life stereotypes and surprisingly sharp commentary on sisterhood betrayed.

sections.content: The film sits within a specific subset of slashers focused on privileged youth facing consequences for past actions. Like I Know What You Did Last Summer (1997), it explores guilt and retribution through the lens of entitled young people trying to protect their futures. The sorority setting allows for examination of toxic friendship dynamics similar to those in Black Christmas (2006) and The House Bunny (2008), though with a darker edge.

What's particularly notable is how Sorority Row bridges old and new slasher conventions. While maintaining traditional elements like creative kills and red herrings, it incorporates modern technology and social dynamics in ways that predecessors like Urban Legend (1998) couldn't explore. The film's commentary on sisterhood bonds versus individual survival mirrors themes in later films like Scream 4 (2011). SUBHEAD: Modern Slasher Evolution

sections.content: The film represents a transition point between classic slasher formulas and contemporary horror sensibilities. While Halloween H20 (1998) brought back legacy characters and Scream (1996) deconstructed the genre, Sorority Row attempted to modernize familiar tropes for a new generation. Its approach to female relationships and power dynamics presaged later films like Happy Death Day (2017) and Ready or Not (2019), which further subverted genre expectations.
